lesson.title: What Counts as an Answer: Every Value That Works
lesson.summary: Learn that the solution set of an equation is the complete collection of values that make it true, and see how that set can contain one number, no numbers, or every number.
lesson.body:
When an equation is solved and a value like x = 3 is found, that single number is technically a member of something larger called the solution set: the complete collection of every value that, when substituted for the variable, makes the equation a true statement. For most linear equations in one variable, that set contains exactly one number, which is why solving usually feels like finding "the answer." But the idea of a solution set is more general than a single number, and understanding it prevents confusion when an equation behaves unexpectedly.

The solution set for the equation x - 4 = 6 is written {10}, using curly braces to show it is a set, containing the single value that makes the equation true. This connects directly to the process of solving equations: every property of equality applied, every step of isolating x, is really a search for the members of this set. Checking a solution, covered elsewhere in this unit, is the same as verifying that a proposed number actually belongs to the solution set, by confirming it makes both sides of the original equation equal.

Solution sets also make it possible to test whether a specific number belongs to an equation's solutions without fully solving the equation first. To check whether 5 belongs to the solution set of 2x - 3 = 7, substitute: 2(5) - 3 = 10 - 3 = 7, which matches the right side, so 5 does belong to the solution set. Testing 4 the same way gives 2(4) - 3 = 8 - 3 = 5, which does not match 7, so 4 is not a member of the solution set. Solving the equation directly confirms there is exactly one member: add 3 to both sides to get 2x = 10, then divide by 2 to get x = 5, so the solution set is {5}, matching what the substitution test already showed.

Not every equation has a solution. Consider x + 5 = x + 8. Subtract x from both sides: 5 = 8. This is a false statement, no matter what x was, which means no value of x could have made the original equation true. The solution set here is empty, written as the empty set symbol or as {}, meaning it contains no numbers at all. This does not indicate a mistake in solving; it correctly reports that this particular equation has no solution.

At the opposite extreme, consider 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6. Distribute the left side: 2x + 6 = 2x + 6. Subtract 2x from both sides: 6 = 6, a true statement regardless of what x is. Substituting any number for x, such as x = 0 or x = 100, makes both sides equal, since the two sides were equivalent expressions all along. The solution set here is all real numbers, meaning every possible value of x belongs to it.

These three outcomes, exactly one number, no numbers, or all real numbers, are the only possibilities for a linear equation in one variable, and they are formally named identity, contradiction, and conditional equation in the sections that follow. Thinking in terms of a solution set, rather than assuming every equation must produce a single tidy number, is what makes those three outcomes make sense instead of feeling like errors.
